doc.title: Winard Harper interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 10, 2014

title: Jazz careers then and now: more venues and bandstand apprenticeships
summary: Harper contrasts the 1980s, with more clubs and bands like Blakey's and Betty Carter's to apprentice in, with today; four years with Carter was like college.

bands.name: Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: If you went to a party and people questioned you about making a career in jazz, and they say well what’s that like, trying to be a jazz musician — do you have an answer for them?

Wow now that’s a big and deep question. Because I think when I was coming along, as a young man coming out of school and stuff, it was different than what it is today. So that’s almost like two totally different worlds. I think at that age, for a lot of us coming out of school I want to say in the 80s, you know it was different. There seemed to be more opportunities and a lot of hope. Now it’s a little tougher.
Well what were the opportunities that were there before that aren’t here now?

Well I think one, first off, there were more venues. There were more places to play. When we came along I could at least say maybe in almost every major city there was at least one club or place that you could hope to play and work. It’s not quite that way today. And then on top of that what a lot of us that came along let’s say late 70s, 80s, there were some bands you could play in. You could go apprentice with somebody. You know Art Blakey was still around; Betty Carter; Horace Silver, that band; Sonny Rollins. I mean that’s just off the top of my head, a few of the bands. And now there’s not enough work for a lot of guys to even keep a regular working band. © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
Yeah, to keep the same group of people together. And you did that.

Yeah. We’re still trying to do that. That’s why I’m saying we’re getting beat up bad. But when we came along, say me and the first band I played in with Betty Carter, me and Benny Green, that was a band we could sit in and work, rehearse, go out of the road, and I did it for four years. Most of us pretty much had like a four year run with her. And the same thing with a lot of guys that worked with Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers — a place you could go sit and hone your craft, learn, for about three or four years.
